name: Ankylosing Spondylitis

ethnicAssociations: Higher prevalence in populations with high HLA-B27 frequency
More common in Northern European and some Native American populations
Lower prevalence in Sub-Saharan African and Japanese populations

diagnosticCriteria.formalCriteriaName: Modified New York Criteria (1984) and ASAS Classification Criteria for Axial SpA (2009)

criteria.description: Low back pain and stiffness > 3 months, improved by exercise and not relieved by rest
Limitation of lumbar spine motion in sagittal and frontal planes
Limitation of chest expansion relative to age and sex
Bilateral sacroiliitis grade >= 2 or unilateral sacroiliitis grade 3-4 on radiograph
Sacroiliitis on imaging (radiograph or MRI) plus >= 1 SpA feature

diagnosticCriteria.minimumForDiagnosis: Modified New York: >= 1 clinical criterion + radiographic sacroiliitis. ASAS axial SpA: Sacroiliitis on imaging + >= 1 SpA feature, OR HLA-B27 + >= 2 SpA features.
diagnosticCriteria.notes: Diagnosis of radiographic axial SpA (ankylosing spondylitis) requires definite sacroiliitis on plain radiograph. Pre-radiographic disease may be classified as non-radiographic axial SpA.

pathognomonic.notes: Insidious onset, age < 40, morning stiffness > 30 min, improves with exercise, not relieved by rest

common.symptomName: Progressive spinal stiffness / reduced lumbar mobility

rare.notes: Aortitis and aortic root dilation in long-standing disease
Very rare complication of long-standing disease

laboratory: HLA-B27 positive in ~90-95% of patients with AS
Elevated CRP and ESR (may be normal in some patients)
imaging: Sacroiliac joint radiographs: bilateral sacroiliitis with sclerosis, erosion, and eventual fusion
MRI sacroiliac joints: bone marrow edema on STIR sequences (early/active disease)
Spinal radiographs: syndesmophytes, squaring of vertebral bodies, 'bamboo spine' in advanced disease
genetic: HLA-B27 (present in ~90-95% of AS patients; ~8% of general population)
ERAP1, IL-23R, and other susceptibility loci identified by GWAS
other: Modified Schober test for lumbar flexion
BASFI and BASDAI clinical scores for disease activity and function

distinguishingFeatures: PsA has psoriatic skin and nail changes
PsA has asymmetric sacroiliitis and peripheral predominance
ReA triggered by preceding infection (urogenital or enteric)
ReA features conjunctivitis more than uveitis
FM has normal inflammatory markers and imaging
FM pain is widespread rather than axial-predominant
FM has no sacroiliitis on imaging

redFlags: Acute eye pain and redness (anterior uveitis - urgent ophthalmology referral)
Spinal fracture after minor trauma (osteoporotic or stress fracture in fused spine)
New neurological symptoms (cauda equina syndrome or spinal cord compression)
Significant constitutional symptoms (fever, weight loss - exclude infection or malignancy)
Rapidly progressive kyphosis or inability to look forward
references: van der Linden S, Valkenburg HA, Cats A. Assessment of the Spondylarthritides. Ann Rheum Dis. 1984;43(3):359-67.
Rudwaleit M, et al. The development of Assessment of SpondyloArthritis international Society classification criteria for axial spondyloarthritis. Ann Rheum Dis. 2009;68(6):777-83.
Sieper J, Poddubnyy D. Axial spondyloarthritis. Lancet. 2017;390(10089):73-84.
Taurog JD, Chhabra A, Colbert RA. Ankylosing spondylitis and axial spondyloarthritis. N Engl J Med. 2016;374(26):2563-74.
